input.strategy_title: Graduate Llama Stack to General Availability
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Llama Stack shipped as Tech Preview and adoption is strong, but enterprise
customers will not build production GenAI applications on a TP component.
Graduating to GA requires API stability commitments, a production support
posture, and closing the quality gaps that TP status currently excuses. The
full inventory of those gaps is not yet known — TP feedback is scattered across
support tickets, and no systematic GA-readiness assessment has been done.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | A GA-readiness assessment inventories the gaps between current TP quality and GA bar (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling), producing the definitive GA scope. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Published API surface carries a stability guarantee: versioned APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the last two TP releases. |
| HLR-3 | P0 | Production support posture is in place: documented SLO targets, backport policy, and supported configuration matrix. |
| HLR-4 | P1 | Safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented integration (not an experimental flag) for GA distributions. |
| HLR-5 | P1 | The Dashboard enables Llama Stack management by default for entitled clusters (no TP opt-in gate). |
| HLR-6 | P2 | Documentation is uplifted to GA standards, including migration notes from TP. |

## Affected Components

- Llama Stack
- TrustyAI
- Dashboard

## Out of Scope

- New Llama Stack feature development beyond GA-bar quality work
- Deprecating alternative GenAI serving paths

## Open Questions

1. The GA scope itself depends on HLR-1's assessment — until it lands, the
   size of the stability and hardening work is an estimate.

# Llama Stack GA-readiness assessment

## Description

This investigation delivers the GA-readiness assessment for Llama Stack: a
systematic inventory of the gaps between current Tech Preview quality and the
GA bar across API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, and error handling,
consolidating TP feedback scattered across support tickets. Its output is the
definitive GA scope that all downstream stability, hardening, and
documentation work is planned against.

## Scope

- Audit the published Llama Stack surface (OpenAI-compatible REST APIs and the
  LlamaStackDistribution CRD) for stability gaps against the GA bar.
- Assess upgrade paths from recent TP releases, identifying breakage and
  migration risks.
- Assess scale limits (concurrency, payload, distribution sizing) and identify
  where limits are unknown, untested, or below GA bar.
- Assess error handling across the distribution (failure detection, error
  surfacing, recovery behavior) and identify gaps.
- Consolidate TP feedback from support tickets into the gap inventory.
- Classify each gap by severity and GA-bar impact, and produce the definitive
  GA scope: the prioritized list of gaps to close for graduation, with a
  recommended disposition per gap (close for GA / defer with justification /
  already covered).
- Structure the output so each downstream work stream (API stability,
  quality hardening, support posture, documentation) can be planned directly
  from it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A GA-readiness assessment report exists covering all four named dimensions
  (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling), with
  current-state evidence for each identified gap.
- Every gap entry carries a severity classification and a recommended
  disposition (in GA scope / deferred / covered), so the report constitutes
  the definitive GA scope for the graduation effort.
- TP support-ticket feedback is consolidated into the inventory, with ticket
  themes reflected as gap items rather than left as raw ticket references.
- The assessment is reviewable by the owning team and downstream work items
  can be derived from it without re-interpreting the source material.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): GA-readiness assessment inventories the gaps between current TP
  quality and the GA bar, producing the definitive GA scope — this epic is the
  direct delivery of HLR-1.

# Llama Stack API stability guarantee and upgrade path

## Description

This epic puts a stability guarantee on Llama Stack's published API surface:
versioned APIs, a documented deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path
from the last two TP releases. It delivers the API-stability portion of the
GA bar identified by the GA-readiness assessment.

## Scope

- Define and apply a versioning scheme to the published API surface of the
  Llama Stack distribution (OpenAI-compatible REST APIs and the
  LlamaStackDistribution CRD).
- Document a deprecation policy for the published surface: how APIs may be
  deprecated or changed, and what users can rely on across releases.
- Build automated upgrade-path tests that verify distribution upgrades from
  the last two TP releases to the GA candidate, covering the surfaces the
  stability guarantee covers.
- Close the API-stability gaps identified by the GA-readiness assessment
  within the published surface.
- Document the stability guarantee itself as part of the published surface
  (what is covered, what is not).

## Acceptance Criteria

- The published API surface of the Llama Stack distribution is versioned, and
  the versioning is visible to consumers of the distribution.
- A deprecation policy is documented and covers the published API surface,
  stated at the level of commitment (no specific notice periods or schemes
  are prescribed here — those are implementation decisions for the team).
- Automated upgrade-path tests exist and pass for upgrades from each of the
  last two TP releases to the GA candidate, running in the project's regular
  build and test pipeline.
- Every API-stability gap that the GA-readiness assessment placed in the GA
  scope for the published surface is closed or carries an agreed, documented
  disposition.
- The stability guarantee is documented and states which surfaces it covers.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): published API surface carries a stability guarantee — versioned
  APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the last two TP
  releases.
- HLR-1 (P0, partial): closes the API-stability and upgrade-path gaps that
  the GA-readiness assessment inventories.

# Close assessed GA-readiness gaps in Llama Stack quality

## Description

This epic closes the quality gaps the GA-readiness assessment places in the
GA scope that are not API-stability work: validated scale limits, error
handling, and any other assessed GA-bar quality gaps in the Llama Stack
distribution. It delivers the "closing the quality gaps that TP status
currently excuses" intent of the strategy.

## Scope

- Remediate the scale-limit gaps identified by the GA-readiness assessment:
  establish, enforce where applicable, and validate the limits the assessment
  placed in GA scope.
- Remediate the assessed error-handling gaps: defined failure detection,
  error surfacing, and recovery behavior for the failure cases in scope.
- Close any other assessed GA-bar quality gaps assigned to quality hardening
  by the assessment's dispositions.
- Add regression coverage for the remediated gaps so the fixes hold across
  releases.
- Record final validated limits and failure behavior so the support posture
  and documentation work can consume them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every gap the GA-readiness assessment placed in the GA scope under quality
  hardening (scale limits, error handling, and other assessed items) is closed
  or carries an agreed, documented disposition.
- Validated scale limits are documented and demonstrably tested for the
  configurations in scope.
- Assessed error-handling gaps have defined failure behavior with test
  coverage demonstrating the behavior.
- The remediation results are recorded in a form the support-posture and
  documentation deliverables can reference (validated limits, failure
  behavior descriptions).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, partial): closes the quality gaps (scale limits, error handling,
  and other inventoried items) that the GA-readiness assessment places in the
  definitive GA scope.

# Llama Stack production support posture

## Description

This epic establishes the production support posture for Llama Stack as a GA
component: documented SLO targets, a backport policy, and a supported
configuration matrix. These are the support-facing commitments that
distinguish GA from Tech Preview.

## Scope

- Define and document SLO targets for the Llama Stack distribution in
  production support terms (the specific target values are decisions for the
  support and product functions, informed by validated behavior).
- Define and document a backport policy: which releases receive fixes and for
  how long, consistent with the platform's GA support model.
- Define and document the supported configuration matrix: the distribution
  versions, providers, deployment configurations, and scale ranges that are
  supported in GA.
- Incorporate the validated scale limits and quality findings into the
  supported configuration matrix: the assessment identifies the limit gaps,
  and the validated, tested limits themselves are recorded by the
  quality-hardening work that closes the assessed gaps (the matrix's
  supported scale-range entries come from that hardening work's recorded
  limits).
- Publish the posture documents through the product's support documentation
  channels.

## Acceptance Criteria

- SLO targets for the Llama Stack distribution are documented and published.
- A backport policy is documented and published.
- A supported configuration matrix is documented and published, and it
  incorporates the validated scale limits and failure behavior recorded by
  the quality-hardening work that closes the assessed GA-readiness gaps (the
  assessment only identifies limit gaps; the validated, tested limits are the
  hardening work's deliverable, which is why that work blocks this epic).
- The posture documents are reviewed and published through the owning support
  documentation process.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P0): production support posture is in place — documented SLO targets,
  backport policy, and supported configuration matrix.

# TrustyAI guardrails integration fail-mode and security analysis

## Description

This investigation analyzes the TrustyAI guardrails integration in Llama
Stack distributions from two angles — its failure modes and its security
posture — and defines what the integration must satisfy to carry supported
status in GA. Promoting a safety guardrails path from an experimental flag
to a supported integration changes its risk profile: production GenAI
applications will rely on it, so what happens when it fails must be known
and specified, and the path between the Llama Stack distribution and
TrustyAI becomes part of the production attack surface of every GA
distribution. Both analyses must land before the integration is hardened.

## Scope

- Enumerate the failure modes of the TrustyAI guardrails integration as
  deployed with a Llama Stack distribution: TrustyAI service unavailability,
  timeouts and slow responses, misconfiguration, partial degradation, and
  guardrail bypass scenarios.
- For each failure mode, document the current (experimental) behavior:
  how the failure is detected, what users of the distribution observe, and
  what happens to guarded requests.
- Define the failure behavior required for supported status per failure mode
  (detection, fallback, and surfacing requirements), as recommendations the
  integration hardening work implements.
- Identify which failure modes block supported status versus which are
  acceptable with documented behavior.
- Review the integration path between a Llama Stack distribution and TrustyAI
  instances: authentication and authorization between the components, data in
  transit, and multi-tenant isolation (the guardrails path spans project
  boundaries by design).
- Review the configuration surface of the integration for insecure defaults
  and misconfiguration risks.
- Catalogue identified vulnerabilities and weaknesses with severity and
  remediation recommendations.
- Determine whether the integration meets the security requirements the
  platform applies to supported GA components, and what (if anything) must be
  remediated before promotion.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A fail-mode inventory exists for the TrustyAI guardrails integration,
  covering unavailability, timeouts, misconfiguration, degradation, and
  bypass scenarios.
- Each failure mode documents current behavior with evidence (source-level or
  runtime), not assumption.
- Each failure mode carries a defined required behavior for supported status,
  or an explicit determination that current behavior is acceptable when
  documented.
- The analysis states which failure modes are blocking for supported status,
  giving the hardening work a concrete pass/fail input.
- A security review of the TrustyAI–Llama Stack guardrails integration path
  exists, covering authentication/authorization, data in transit, and
  multi-tenant isolation.
- Identified weaknesses are catalogued with severity and concrete remediation
  recommendations.
- The review states a determination of whether the integration meets the
  security bar for supported status in GA distributions, with the blocking
  items (if any) identified.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1, supporting): TrustyAI guardrails as a supported integration for
  GA distributions — this investigation resolves the fail-mode and security
  unknowns that gate the hardening of that integration.

# TrustyAI guardrails as supported Llama Stack integration

## Description

This epic promotes the TrustyAI guardrails integration from an experimental
flag to a supported integration for Llama Stack GA distributions. It hardens
the integration per the fail-mode and security analysis outcomes, adds
qualification coverage, and captures the technical facts the GA user
documentation needs (configuration, failure behavior, support scope) as an
input to the documentation work.

## Scope

- Promote the TrustyAI guardrails integration out of the experimental flag in
  GA distributions of Llama Stack.
- Implement (or verify and document) the failure behavior required by the
  fail-mode analysis for each blocking failure mode, including detection and
  surfacing of guardrails failures to users of the distribution.
- Remediate the security findings the security analysis identified as blocking
  for supported status, or document accepted risk with justification.
- Add qualification test coverage for the integration in supported
  configurations, covering normal operation and the failure behavior defined
  by the fail-mode analysis.
- Capture the technical facts required for the integration's user-facing GA

  Dashboard's existing feature-flag configuration, demonstrating a rollback
  path for the default flip.

  GA-candidate Llama Stack distribution (verified in the epic's testing, not
  deferred to users).

107	1. Different component OR different team → separate epics
108	2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:
109	   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.
110	   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.
111	   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.
112	
113	### Investigation Edges
114	3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.
115	4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.
116	
117	### Implementation Type Ordering
118	5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)
119	6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). Doesn't block other repos.
120	7. `license-validation` ∥ `repo-onboarding` parallel (independent inputs)
121	8. `license-validation` ∥ `konflux-onboarding` parallel (config doesn't depend on specific deps)
122	9. `license-validation` → general implementation serial (if licenses fail, deps change, affects approach)
123	10. `konflux-onboarding` ∥ general implementation parallel (config independent of code; AC gates first execution). **Add NO blocking edge in either direction.** It is tempting to make the general implementation depend on `konflux-onboarding` ("the code needs a build pipeline first") — do not. That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 "build pipeline green" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation. This holds for EVERY `konflux-onboarding` × general-implementation pair in the decomposition, whatever the general epic's component or deliverable — a stack-wide assembly, packaging, or evidence epic that consumes the pipeline's outputs is still a general implementation. There is no "different component" or "genuine artifact dependency" exemption: if the coupling is real, express it as an AC on the consuming epic ("the signed attestations from the build pipeline are included and validated"), never as an edge.
124	11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.
125	
126	### Implementation → Implementation Edges
127	12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)
128	13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a "pinned image digest available" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel. The same holds for any build-pipeline output another epic consumes as CONTENT — signed attestations, SBOMs, provenance, scan results: the consuming epic gets an AC ("the evidence package includes the signed attestations produced by the build pipeline"), not an edge. Code builds against an API, CRD, or library; it does not build against attestations or digests.
129	14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel
130	15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)
131

133	16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)
134	17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)
135	18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)

138	19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation

For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).

150	When an external dependency has uncertain timing:

152	1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?
153	2. **YES** → Split into:

158	## Step 6: Classify Epics
159	
160	For each epic, determine:
161	
162	### Type (mandatory)
163	- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)
164	- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)
165	
166	### Implementation Type (optional routing label)
167	
168	| Label | When to apply |
169	|-------|--------------|
170	| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |
171	| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |
172	| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |
173	| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |
174	| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |

176	### AI Implementability Signals
177	
178	Score signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.
179	
180	#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)
181	
182	Evaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.
183	
184	| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |
185	|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|
186	| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope ("improve X") |
187	| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |
188	| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |
189	| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |
190	| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |
191	| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |
192	| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |
193	| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |
194	| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |
195	
196	**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state ("shipped as Tech Preview", "generally available"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word "claim". A strategy premise that drives the decomposition (e.g. a maturity gap motivating a hardening program) is an architecture claim. Check `.context/architecture-context/` for the epic's components: score +1 when a context file corroborates the premise or grounds the epic's scope, and cite that file in the rationale; score -1 when the strategy asserts something the context contradicts; score 0 only when no context file covers any component the epic touches. "The strategy makes no specific architecture claims" is not a valid 0 rationale when context files exist for the components in scope.
197	
198	#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)
199	
200	**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.
201	
202	| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |
203	|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|
204	| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |
205	| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |
206	| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |
207	| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |
208	| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. "is this ADR approved?") |
209	
210	The pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.

212	Write the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.

214	## Step 6.5: Health Warnings
215	
216	### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)
217	- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)
218	- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent
219	- Epic size overages kept deliberately: when you keep an epic above the ~2-week guideline because it is one logical change (a split would duplicate an audit or fragment a single mechanical pass over one surface), the Health Warning must carry a **re-split trigger** — the concrete, measurable planning condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. "re-split along sub-system lines if the call-site audit finds materially more sites than the estimate"). A justified overage with a recorded trigger is a managed trade-off; a bare "above guideline, noted for planning awareness" note is an unresolved defect that the review will dock and the contract validator will flag.

221	### Handling unclear strategy passages
222	
223	When the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:
224	
225	| Situation | Handling |
226	|-----------|---------|
227	| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |
228	| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |
229	
230	When a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, "if X requires changes to Y"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.

## Step 0: Triage

Read the strategy file. Run these checks in order; first match terminates the flow:

**Check 1 — Below threshold**: If the strategy is S-sized AND affects a single component AND a single team AND ≥67% of scope would score High AI implementability — check two escape conditions before triggering:

- **Genuine unknowns**: If the strategy contains open questions, conditional ADRs, or pending reviews where the answer would change which epics exist or what they do, below-threshold does not apply. Proceed to Step 1 so Investigation epics can be created.
- **Multiple distinct work streams**: If the scope spans architecturally distinct sub-systems that warrant separate PR review cycles (e.g., backend API + frontend UI, or code implementation + substantive content authoring + documentation), below-threshold does not apply. Proceed to Step 1 — these splits are architectural, not priority-based, and produce better-scoped PRs. **Incidental documentation touch-ups do not count as a distinct work stream.** Updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of the same change — with no new content authored — stays in the single epic (as scope/acceptance criteria) and does not defeat below-threshold. Only *substantive* content authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, or new/rewritten doc topics) is a distinct work stream.

If neither escape condition applies: produce a single epic file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md` (with full frontmatter and body per Step 8) and a decomposition summary. Then stop — no DAG, no multi-step decomposition. Do not proceed to Steps 1-8. In particular, Step 4's priority-split logic does not apply: a below-threshold strategy stays as one epic even if its HLRs span multiple priority levels.

**Check 2 — Documentation only**: If all affected components have "No code changes" or "reference only": produce a single epic file with `implementation_type: docs-authoring`, content outline, and mandatory accuracy validation against architecture context. Write the decomposition summary. Then stop.

For either triage path, write the epic file per Step 8b, run the contract validator (`python3 skills/epic-decompose/scripts/validate_decomposition.py {ID}` — fix any `VIOLATION:` it reports before continuing), then set summary frontmatter and the completion sentinel:

```bash
python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \
    parent_strat="{ID}" epic_count=1 critical_path_length=1 \
    triage=below-threshold triage_rationale="<reason>"

python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true
```

Use `triage=docs-only` for Check 2. The `decompose_complete=true` line must be your **final action** — the pipeline will not launch the review agent until it is set.

If neither check fires, proceed to Step 1.

## Step 1: Parse Strategy Structure

Extract these sections from the strategy:

- **Affected Components table**: (component name, what changes, owner team)
- **Impacted Teams table**: (team, components owned, involvement)
- **High Level Requirements**: with P0/P1/P2 priority
- **Dependencies table**: (dependency, type, status, impact if blocked)
- **Acceptance Criteria**: (Given/When/Then with "measured by" clauses)
- **Non-Functional Requirements**

If any required section is missing, note it as a health warning but proceed with available information.

## Step 1.5: Parse Staff Engineer Input

If the strategy contains a Staff Engineer Input section that is non-empty (beyond template placeholder text):

- Parse it first — it takes precedence
- When Staff Engineer Input diverges from AI-generated Technical Approach, use the Staff Engineer Input
- Log each override for traceability in the decomposition summary

## Step 2: Build Component Graph

**Component name constraint:** Read `.context/rhai-components.txt` for the canonical list of RHAI Jira components. Every epic's `component` value MUST be copied verbatim from this list — never invented, paraphrased, or combined ("Model Serving Stack" is invalid; the canonical list has `Serving Runtimes`). Match the strategy's Affected Components to the closest canonical name; when one epic's work spans several strategy components, assign the single most-relevant canonical name and note the span in the decomposition summary. `submit.py` silently strips any component not in the list, leaving the Jira epic component-less. Log any non-obvious mappings in the decomposition summary.

For each (component, change, owner team) tuple from the Affected Components table:

**Active vs. Passive classification:**
- **Active component**: Code changes needed → generates epic(s)
- **Passive component**: No code changes, keep working → validation becomes acceptance criterion on nearest active component's epic
- **Exception**: If a different team validates the passive component → generate a separate validation Implementation epic owned by that team

**New component detection:**
- Check `.context/architecture-context/` for component existence
- Component is "in platform" if an architecture context file exists for it
- Component NOT in architecture context → create:
  - Implementation epic(s) for provisioning with appropriate `implementation_type`
  - Investigation epic if dependency availability needs validation

## Step 3: Identify Investigation Epics

First, systematically scan the strategy for all unknowns — check the open questions table, risks table, assumptions, pending reviews, and conditional ADRs. Do not rely on the technical approach section alone; open questions are often in tables at the end of the strategy and may contradict or qualify the detailed technical description.

Collect the full list of unknowns before creating any Investigation epics. Then evaluate each independently:

**Decision rule: Does the answer change which downstream epics exist or what they do?**

- **YES** → Investigation epic. Determine which downstream epics depend on the outcome. Add as DAG edges. For bounded outcomes (≤3 possibilities): output conditional decomposition branches.
- **NO** → Acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic. Implementation proceeds the same way regardless; failure = fix-and-retry.

Multiple independent unknowns can produce multiple Investigation epics, even for the same component and team. The component/team boundary rule applies to Implementations (bundling work for a team), not Investigations (resolving a specific unknown). However, if two qualifying unknowns would be resolved by the same experiment producing the same deliverable, combine them into one Investigation — don't split for the sake of splitting.

## Step 4: Map HLRs to Epics

**Precondition:** This step only runs for strategies that were NOT triaged in Step 0. If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.

- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics
- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements
- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables
- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0
- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries. When you keep a lower-priority HLR bundled, record the bundling where the mapping is read: in the HLR Traceability Matrix, flag that HLR's row as `bundled` and state inline why it is not separately schedulable (it edits the same call sites, data structure, or surface as the higher-priority work — splitting would double-touch them). The row-level flag is what shows a reviewer the priority label was analyzed rather than collapsed; a rationale that lives only in a distant prose section does not.
- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. "select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side" and "a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.
- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.

## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG

Apply these rules to construct edges between epics:

### Epic Boundary Rules
1. Different component OR different team → separate epics
2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:
   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.
   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.
   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.

### Investigation Edges
3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.
4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.

### Implementation Type Ordering
5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)
6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). Doesn't block other repos.
7. `license-validation` ∥ `repo-onboarding` parallel (independent inputs)
8. `license-validation` ∥ `konflux-onboarding` parallel (config doesn't depend on specific deps)
9. `license-validation` → general implementation serial (if licenses fail, deps change, affects approach)
10. `konflux-onboarding` ∥ general implementation parallel (config independent of code; AC gates first execution). **Add NO blocking edge in either direction.** It is tempting to make the general implementation depend on `konflux-onboarding` ("the code needs a build pipeline first") — do not. That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 "build pipeline green" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation. This holds for EVERY `konflux-onboarding` × general-implementation pair in the decomposition, whatever the general epic's component or deliverable — a stack-wide assembly, packaging, or evidence epic that consumes the pipeline's outputs is still a general implementation. There is no "different component" or "genuine artifact dependency" exemption: if the coupling is real, express it as an AC on the consuming epic ("the signed attestations from the build pipeline are included and validated"), never as an edge.
11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.

### Implementation → Implementation Edges
12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)
13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a "pinned image digest available" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel. The same holds for any build-pipeline output another epic consumes as CONTENT — signed attestations, SBOMs, provenance, scan results: the consuming epic gets an AC ("the evidence package includes the signed attestations produced by the build pipeline"), not an edge. Code builds against an API, CRD, or library; it does not build against attestations or digests.
14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel
15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)

### External Dependency Edges
16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)
17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)
18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)

### Epic Generation Rules
19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation
20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).
21. External community dependency where team submits PR/RFC and acceptance gates downstream → generate upstream Implementation epic, evaluate tiered delivery. If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.
22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation

### Acceptance Criteria Rules
23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic
24. `docs-authoring` epic → add "technically reviewed against implementation" AC
25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add "build pipeline green" AC

## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery

When an external dependency has uncertain timing:

1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?
2. **YES** → Split into:
   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)
   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)
3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream

## Step 6: Classify Epics

For each epic, determine:

### Type (mandatory)
- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)
- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)

### Implementation Type (optional routing label)

| Label | When to apply |
|-------|--------------|
| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |
| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |
| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |
| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |
| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |

### AI Implementability Signals

Score signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.

#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)

Evaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.

| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |
|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|
| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope ("improve X") |
| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |
| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |
| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |
| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |
| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |
| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |
| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |
| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |

**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state ("shipped as Tech Preview", "generally available"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word "claim". A strategy premise that drives the decomposition (e.g. a maturity gap motivating a hardening program) is an architecture claim. Check `.context/architecture-context/` for the epic's components: score +1 when a context file corroborates the premise or grounds the epic's scope, and cite that file in the rationale; score -1 when the strategy asserts something the context contradicts; score 0 only when no context file covers any component the epic touches. "The strategy makes no specific architecture claims" is not a valid 0 rationale when context files exist for the components in scope.

#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)

**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.

| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |
|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|
| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |
| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |
| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |
| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |
| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. "is this ADR approved?") |

The pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.

Write the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.

## Step 6.5: Health Warnings

### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)
- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)
- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent
- Epic size overages kept deliberately: when you keep an epic above the ~2-week guideline because it is one logical change (a split would duplicate an audit or fragment a single mechanical pass over one surface), the Health Warning must carry a **re-split trigger** — the concrete, measurable planning condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. "re-split along sub-system lines if the call-site audit finds materially more sites than the estimate"). A justified overage with a recorded trigger is a managed trade-off; a bare "above guideline, noted for planning awareness" note is an unresolved defect that the review will dock and the contract validator will flag.

### Handling unclear strategy passages

When the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:

| Situation | Handling |
|-----------|---------|
| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |
| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |

When a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, "if X requires changes to Y"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.

## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria

Each epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:
- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope
- HLRs mapped to this epic
- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)
- Rules 23-25 from Step 5

Every AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable — something the epic's engineering work produces or verifies. Externally-controlled preconditions are not ACs, in either form: schedule constraints (turnaround you do not control — accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) or availability preconditions (procurement, dedicated hardware or node allocation, partner-lab access, environment provisioning) — anything granted by parties outside the strategy belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — "the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged" is a valid AC; "lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC; "dedicated hardware nodes are available to the campaign" is an availability precondition misfiled as an AC — the epic's work may include *securing* access, but the access being granted is not a condition the epic's deliverable produces, so it stays in Risks/Notes while the AC sits on the deliverable itself (e.g. the campaign's validated report).

## Step 8: Generate Artifacts

### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)

Write the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.

Write `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:

1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:
   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)
   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means "E001 must complete before E003 can start")
   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)
   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)
   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)
   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)

2. Set frontmatter via script:

```bash
python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \
    parent_strat="{ID}" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>
```

Add `triage=<value> triage_rationale="<reason>"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).

### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design

Your job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.
If the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.
Do not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,
CRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions
for the implementing team.

### Step 8b: Write per-epic files

Write one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.

For each epic, write in two steps:

1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):
   - **Title** (one line)
   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)
   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)
   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)
   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)
   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).
   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.

   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., "E001", "E003") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Draft IDs are internal to the decomposition and meaningless once epics are created in Jira. Dependency relationships are captured by frontmatter `dependencies` and Jira Blocks links. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., "the OTEL env var injection capability" not "E003") without naming sibling epics.

2. Set frontmatter via script:

```bash
python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \
    epic_id="{ID}-E001" title="<epic title>" parent_strat="{ID}" \
    component="<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>" team="<owner team>" \
    type=Implementation priority=P0 \
    dependencies="{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003" \
    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \
    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \
    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \
    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \
    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \
    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \
    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \
    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \
    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1
```

For an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five
`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):

```bash
python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \
    epic_id="{ID}-E001" title="<epic title>" parent_strat="{ID}" \
    component="<canonical name>" team="<owner team>" \
    type=Investigation priority=P0 \
    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \
    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \
    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \
    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \
    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0
```

Add optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach="<text>"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).

Do **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.

### Step 8c: Verify consistency

After writing all epic files, run:
```
python3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md
```

Compare the output against the decomposition summary. If any epic file's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, or HLR mappings diverged from the plan, fix the epic file to match the summary.

Then run the contract validator until it passes:

```bash

A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation. This holds for EVERY `konflux-onboarding` × general-implementation pair in the decomposition, whatever the general epic's component or deliverable — a stack-wide assembly, packaging, or evidence epic that consumes the pipeline's outputs is still a general implementation. There is no "different component" or "genuine artifact dependency" exemption: if the coupling is real, express it as an AC on the consuming epic ("the signed attestations from the build pipeline are included and validated"), never as an edge.
124	11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.
125	
126	### Implementation → Implementation Edges
127	12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)
128	13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a "pinned image digest available" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel. The same holds for any build-pipeline output another epic consumes as CONTENT — signed attestations, SBOMs, provenance, scan results: the consuming epic gets an AC ("the evidence package includes the signed attestations produced by the build pipeline"), not an edge. Code builds against an API, CRD, or library; it does not build against attestations or digests.
129	14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel
130	15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)
131	
132	### External Dependency Edges
133	16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)
134	17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)
135	18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)
136	
137	### Epic Generation Rules
138	19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation
139	20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).

If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.
141	22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation
142	
143	### Acceptance Criteria Rules
144	23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic
145	24. `docs-authoring` epic → add "technically reviewed against implementation" AC
146	25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add "build pipeline green" AC

148	## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery
149	
150	When an external dependency has uncertain timing:
151	
152	1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?
153	2. **YES** → Split into:
154	   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)
155	   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)
156	3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream
157	
158	## Step 6: Classify Epics
159	
160	For each epic, determine:
161	
162	### Type (mandatory)
163	- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)
164	- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)
165	
166	### Implementation Type (optional routing label)
167	
168	| Label | When to apply |
169	|-------|--------------|
170	| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |
171	| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |
172	| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |
173	| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |
174	| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |
175	
176	### AI Implementability Signals
177	
178	Score signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.
179	
180	#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)
181	
182	Evaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.
183	
184	| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |
185	|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|
186	| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope ("improve X") |
187	| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |
188	| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |
189	| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |
190	| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |
191	| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |
192	| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |
193	| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |
194	| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |
195	
196	**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state ("shipped as Tech Preview", "generally available"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word "claim". A strategy premise that drives the decomposition (e.g. a maturity gap motivating a hardening program) is an architecture claim. Check `.context/architecture-context/` for the epic's components: score +1 when a context file corroborates the premise or grounds the epic's scope, and cite that file in the rationale; score -1 when the strategy asserts something the context contradicts; score 0 only when no context file covers any component the epic touches. "The strategy makes no specific architecture claims" is not a valid 0 rationale when context files exist for the components in scope.
197	
198	#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)
199	
200	**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.
201	
202	| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |
203	|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|
204	| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |
205	| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |
206	| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |
207	| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |
208	| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. "is this ADR approved?") |
209	
210	The pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.
211	
212	Write the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.

214	## Step 6.5: Health Warnings
215	
216	### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)
217	- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)
218	- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent
219	- Epic size overages kept deliberately: when you keep an epic above the ~2-week guideline because it is one logical change (a split would duplicate an audit or fragment a single mechanical pass over one surface), the Health Warning must carry a **re-split trigger** — the concrete, measurable planning condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. "re-split along sub-system lines if the call-site audit finds materially more sites than the estimate"). A justified overage with a recorded trigger is a managed trade-off; a bare "above guideline, noted for planning awareness" note is an unresolved defect that the review will dock and the contract validator will flag.
220	
221	### Handling unclear strategy passages
222	
223	When the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:
224	
225	| Situation | Handling |
226	|-----------|---------|
227	| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |
228	| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |
229	
230	When a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, "if X requires changes to Y"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.

232	## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria
233	
234	Each epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:
235	- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope
236	- HLRs mapped to this epic
237	- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)
238	- Rules 23-25 from Step 5
239	
240	Every AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable — something the epic's engineering work produces or verifies. Externally-controlled preconditions are not ACs, in either form: schedule constraints (turnaround you do not control — accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) or availability preconditions (procurement, dedicated hardware or node allocation, partner-lab access, environment provisioning) — anything granted by parties outside the strategy belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — "the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged" is a valid AC; "lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC; "dedicated hardware nodes are available to the campaign" is an availability precondition misfiled as an AC — the epic's work may include *securing* access, but the access being granted is not a condition the epic's deliverable produces, so it stays in Risks/Notes while the AC sits on the deliverable itself (e.g. the campaign's validated report).

12	## Problem Statement
13	
14	Llama Stack shipped as Tech Preview and adoption is strong, but enterprise
15	customers will not build production GenAI applications on a TP component.
16	Graduating to GA requires API stability commitments, a production support
17	posture, and closing the quality gaps that TP status currently excuses. The
18	full inventory of those gaps is not yet known — TP feedback is scattered across
19	support tickets, and no systematic GA-readiness assessment has been done.
20	
21	## High-Level Requirements
22	
23	| ID | Priority | Requirement |
24	|-------|----------|-------------|
25	| HLR-1 | P0 | A GA-readiness assessment inventories the gaps between current TP quality and GA bar (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling), producing the definitive GA scope. |
26	| HLR-2 | P0 | Published API surface carries a stability guarantee: versioned APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the last two TP releases. |
27	| HLR-3 | P0 | Production support posture is in place: documented SLO targets, backport policy, and supported configuration matrix. |
28	| HLR-4 | P1 | Safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented integration (not an experimental flag) for GA distributions. |
29	| HLR-5 | P1 | The Dashboard enables Llama Stack management by default for entitled clusters (no TP opt-in gate). |
30	| HLR-6 | P2 | Documentation is uplifted to GA standards, including migration notes from TP. |
